stories.title: What We Can Save In A Time Of Endings
stories.summary: The post What We Can Save In A Time Of Endings appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
During the slow disintegrations of the climate crisis, choices about what to preserve become politically and culturally fraught.

Kat Hill is a writer and researcher based in Scotland. Her forthcoming book is “ Endlings: A Journey into the Last of Things .” She has held fellowships and positions at numerous academic institutions including the Institute for Advanced Study and Oxford University. She is currently the creative director of Upland Arts Development in Scotland.

Nicholas J.R. White is a photographer living on the Isle of Skye. He is a recipient of the Royal Photographic Society Environmental Bursary and is the 2026 Ampersand Foundation/Photoworks Fellow.

HAPPISBURGH, England — Off the coast of Norfolk on edge of the North Sea, the ocean can seem calm, but the waters are deceptive. Beneath the marbled brown, lie sand banks and submerged mountains waiting to ensnare unsuspecting ships. Happisburgh (pronounced Hays-burro) is a small, pretty town, its narrow roads lined by houses with walls made of flint pressed into mortar. The beach roads all have names like Stone’s Throw or Cliff Top, and the sea has always been present in people’s lives. But inching ever closer for years, now its incursions are rapid and frightening.

The light changed suddenly. Over my shoulder, the sky was dark with rain that towered in hazy columns against a thunderous glow. It rolled over the beach, over the houses, falling into the sea, billowing over the crumbling cliff edge. Lightning split the blackness, and the clouds rumbled. Gulls soared like scraps of loose paper, and sand martins wheeled in a frenzy, seeking refuge. For a moment, the world had ended. Then, it was clear again: sun shining, birds calling, people laughing.

I was looking out to submerged places, out to the infamous Doggerland. Places with names and identities that no longer exist here. Not in the way they used to. Under the water, now lost to the waves, they live on in their cartographic afterlife. Eccles-on-Sea is named after a church, but the original place of worship is long gone, and the collection of bungalows that form the village hunker behind protecting dunes and a sea wall. This is the Bush Estate, a so-called Plotland community, the name given to settlements that emerged during an early 20th century movement of working-class people buying cheap land on the seaside. Most of the houses, along with St. Mary’s church, were washed away in the 17th century; for a time, only the tower remained, the sea creeping closer and sand drifting over the stones at its base. For years, it acted as a sailor’s beacon until it too succumbed to the waves. Now, only a fragment of the bottom wall apparently remains visible at a low spring tide, though I did not see it. Dunwich, a thriving port town just to the south along the coast, was swept to sea centuries earlier.

They remain a warning to us all of what may befall a place, consigned to ruin, memory and legend.

We live at a time when endings are all around us. But endings are never straightforward. An ending may be made up of many moments. Sometimes, we don’t know when things have truly receded from our world, and it can be difficult to determine what to care about, how and when. Questions about what to save become terribly real.

Standing on the Norfolk coast, I thought how odd it was to both observe an ending and to be caught up in it. In one sense, the decline is apparent and unavoidable: Cliffs have crumbled, houses are gone, the end has happened. But in another, it’s an ending in a constant process of becoming, never starting or finishing, always ongoing. Such a loss carries emotional and philosophical weight across time, where salvation and survival ebb and flow.

The communities here seemed to be in the middle of a slow war, waiting for an enemy who would inevitably arrive no matter what watch they keep. It was an apocalyptic feeling: dark skies, rock defenses, the bones of former homes, tumbledown walls and shattered fences. And yet, the apocalypse seemed simultaneously distant, like a thing of fable, impossible to actually happen.

Writing after World War I, after the destruction wrought on the confidence of Europe, essayist Paul Valéry reflected: “W ⁠ e had long heard tell of whole worlds that had vanished, of empires sunk without a trace. … But the disasters that had sent them down were, after all, none of our affair. Elam, Nineveh, Babylon were but beautiful vague names.” Yet then, he too felt that same fear of collapse after witnessing the horror of war and the devastated world that came after. “We are aware now that a civilisation has the same fragility as a life.” Worlds can end. Choose to look, and absence and scars tell stories.

“No one wants to be made to give something up or be told it’s time to surrender.”

“How can we learn to die?” the philosophers Fernando Flores and B. Scot Rousse asked. But confronting us today is not just individual death, nor even the prospect of human extinction, but the possibility of the disappearance of all our ways of life and being. This is what Jonathan Lear called ontological vulnerability, the sense that a world of meaning might collapse. His book “Radical Hope” was focused on the Crow people of the American West and referred to an “uncanny sense of menace … a shared vulnerability that we cannot quite name.” As Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow, said shortly before he died in 1932: “When the buffalo went away the hearts of my people fell to the ground, and they could not lift them up again. After this nothing happened.”

On the Norfolk coast, the pub, the church, the road and the shop might all soon be gone. Maybe the homes will remain, maybe not. Climate change may not kill everyone, but it may destroy the things that give life meaning. It’s one thing to survive, another to live. When you know that the flood will rush in, the fire will burn, the end is coming, what would you do? And what would you save? One option is to improve defenses: shelter cities and rebuff the rising tide from California to Yorkshire to Pacific islands. Another solution is to move.

In the U.K., the Shoreline Management Plans (SMPs), a series of complex strategic outlines, determine the futures of coastal regions, weighing up priority places to spend money and build walls. They read like military plans. The options are do nothing, maintain defenses, extend defenses or realign coastal assets. Hold the line. Fortify. Resist. Retreat.

In some instances, we have no choice but to protect something because it would do too much damage to leave it undefended. There are nuclear power plants in vulnerable places along the U.K. coast. Sizewell B in Suffolk had been slated to be decommissioned by 2035 but was recently given a new lease of life until 2055; Sizewell C, is newly under construction and due to be operational in the 2030s. It has an elaborate defense plan: raised up on a 7-meter (23-foot) platform with walls. Some say it’s not high enough. Modeling of sea level rise goes to 2140 and doesn’t take into account the long future of nuclear waste. Moreover, walls and floodgates were designed for receding high waters, not permanent rise. They endanger places nearby by preventing the natural movement of sand.

Sellafield, on the Cumbrian Coast, is the most dangerous nuclear site in Europe. It’s always present, the golf ball dome and the chimneys looming in the distance, a crumbling facade behind the farm shops and fells of the Lake District. At night the lights glow with an ominous red haze. It is a hazardous place. High-level waste is stored in legacy silos and ponds. The Magnox Swarf Silo is just leaking into the ground. ⁠ Just down the road, with armored fences on the edge of people’s homes, is the LLW Repository, the dumping ground for all low-level nuclear waste in the U.K. Long-term, the authorities aim to bury all this in the sea, deep down in a Geological Disposal Facility. But for now, they shore them up against the rising sea because to do otherwise would risk it all leaching out in catastrophic fashion. Toxic waste that never becomes safe and cannot be moved will have to be fortified.

The houses on Braystones Beach below Sellafield will not be afforded the same protection. Once, they were railway carriages that brought and housed the workers to build the line along the coast; now, some have been developed into dwellings. Like the Plotland homes of Norfolk, they are marginal communities, places pushed to the edge. Winter high tides have a 7-meter (23-foot) range, with storms whipping up surging waves, ⁠ and the row of single-story dwellings will often have the sea lapping at their doors; rocks and buoys, dredged up and dragged into shore, crash against homes. The inhabitants are determined to stay: They like living here in the wildness and wind. It’s part of the attraction, one woman told me, but they have resorted to building their own walls by claiming boulders and piling gravel and stones into embankments in front of their homes. I stood on the hill above and the small low-slung huts looked like a wall surrounding a fortress, a kind of defense protecting the aging nuclear plant. The Cumbria Coastal Strategy is dismissive of the value of the huts: “The majority of the frontage is undefended and there is no economic justification to providing significant investment at the present time.”

Famously, in 2019, the media condemned a seaside village in Wales called Fairbourne to be abandoned to the sea. House prices plummeted overnight, investment trickled away and the residents were labeled as Britain’s first climate refugees. Locals mobilized against the process of “managed retreat,” but the reputational damage was done and trust was destroyed. Insurance policies, which after all are a bet on the future, often will no longer cover homes in these coastal places.

“Choose to look and absence and scars tell stories.”

There are already ruins and remnants aplenty on the Norfolk coast. It’s littered with the remains of Norman castles and military lookouts. Of all the things we could protect, is it worth saving ruins? Should we simply let them be committed to the memory of the sea? They are more than crumbling walls or upturned pillboxes — they are reminders of our past, anchors that root us to a sense of history and landscape. Just like with everything else, there’ll only be certain ruins designated as important and worth protecting. This is true of any heritage site, not just those threatened by climate change. As Gavin Lucas writes, “entropy is a social as well as a natural phenomenon.”

A recent National Trust report admitted it could not contain threats to coastal sites and aims to work “with the grain of nature.” On the coast of Caithness in Scotland’s far northeast, there are castles at every bay and promontory exposed to the ravages of the sea. One, Castle Sinclair Girnigoe, an impressive northern fortress, was listed on the World Monument Fund’s Monuments Watch in 2002. The complex of structures, dating back to the 15th century and once owned by Clan Sinclair, has received funds to stabilize and conserve the structure. Just along the coast, however, is Castle Bucholie, listed by Historic Environment Scotland, but without the same resources to protect it from its fate. Read Noema in print.

“Old” ruins were once homes or lives. The world is ephemeral. Preservation suggests we can protect things in the future by putting them on lists, but that’s not really true. The Caithness castles lean into the sea, and the empty windows look out to the water like screaming faces. Girnigoe Sinclair reopened with much fanfare in 2010, but the slow creep of time continues regardless of how much attention is given to it. Transience may be an opportunity to tell complex stories though; “managed ruination” can be a way to write what the cultural geographer Caitlin DeSilvey refers to as an “anticipatory history” of absence.

When I visited, Castle Sinclair’s wooden drawbridge was closed and the walls were covered in scaffolding. It is being reclaimed not just by the sea but by nature. Nesting fulmars stared from a window, and marsh orchids were growing out of the turf that covered the ruined walls.

Sea level rise and climate change threaten the nonhuman world, too. I saw ringed plovers on the beach near Sellafield, sand martins on the crumbling cliffs of the Norfolk coast. Signs warn people away from their nesting sites.

Norfolk’s water systems — the great expanses of the Broads, mudflats and marshes — are increasingly susceptible to the incursion of salty waves. The complex estuarine networks are like arteries that get pumped full of seawater when storm surges come. Salty waters kill invertebrates on which nesting waders feed, and wash away habitat.

Nonhuman environments are being squeezed, but who wants to save the sand martins or the butterflies when homes and businesses are at risk? Something must be sacrificed, and “sacrifice zone” is a term becoming increasingly common in discussions about environmental justice. It’s a word in the language of sanctity, martyrdom and faith — an act of giving something up to a higher purpose, to a god or to a devil. It asks that we think about death as something. It asks that we consider who to make a victim. If we build sea walls, we destroy marshland. If we protect nuclear waste, we condemn coastal communities.

No one wants to be made to give something up or be told it’s time to surrender. As I talked to people in Norfolk, Cumbria and Scotland, the rising sea was ever present in their minds, yet they were also persistent and stubborn. This was their home. What else were they supposed to do?

Endings are not neat, and it’s unclear when an ending is inevitable, when it is declared and who gets to declare it. Sometimes a world comes and goes in an instant but, more often, there is a slow disintegration of crumbling and drifting. Despite it all, it’s not easy to leave the thing that gives your world meaning and stability.

On a beach railing I found on the coast of Norfolk, there’s a sticker of a man. Rocks and flowers are arranged around the picture, with words of affectionate remembrance. Nearby is a bench with an inscription to a young biker who loved the view of the sea. The bench and the flowers will be gone soon, such small but momentous reminders of the persistence of love and memory in absence. Is this the time, when past and memory are done, when “nothing happens”?

“Sometimes the world may come and go in an instant but more often there is a slow disintegration of crumbling and drifting.”

Because that’s the thing about these decisions. They are not just cold calculations, but about love, even when an end comes. The residents in Happisburgh and nearby Mundesley are worried about the churches that are threatened by the sea, which will undermine the graves of their family members and community. At St. Mary’s in Happisburgh, there’s a mass grave for sailors who drowned in the deep. Their bones are now being returned to the sea, and with them the memory of their lives.

I wandered into the church and saw a woman tending to the flowers on the altar, a wheelbarrow full of blooms next to her. In a pew, a man sat watching her as the sun streamed in through the glass, illuminating the dancing dust. Richard and Joan have lived and worked here all their lives, both baptized in the centuries-old font.

“One day the sea will take it.” That’s what she says. She knows this is true but she tends the church anyway because it is part of her past. It dates to the 14th century; its peal of eight bells ring every Wednesday. There are legends around here that you can hear the drowned bells of Dunwich or Eccles-on-Sea. I’ve heard a similar tale of the mythical city of Ys, submerged beneath the waves, whose cathedral bell still rings.

There’s another bell on the beach at Happisburgh, designed by artist Marcus Vergette, that rings with the tide. Vergette told me that the bell was the perfect design for the sea. Bells disrupt space. They have a history and personality; they have names. Bells rang for death and life, funeral and marriage, celebration, announcement, mourning or warning. They communicate the passing of time and the ritual of life, and a bell’s back and forthness expresses the liminality of the coast. It is, he said, a particularly suitable form for the shifting sands of life, and to express the ambiguity of loss and desire.

I stood on the beach and listened to it. It tolled for time, for tide, for life and death. It was a liturgy of loss, but it was also a celebration and a call to joy and worship, perhaps even hope or the new dawn of a day.

What hope could it ring for? Lear believed in the vulnerability of our world but also a kind of radical hope even in absence and loss. Perhaps those places that are gone could have an afterlife. Recently archaeologists recorded oral histories around Happisburgh and scanned and 3D-photographed the church so it can live on in some form. Whole countries are adopting this approach. Tuvalu, a Pacific Island nation comprising small islets and low-lying atolls, is aiming to become the first “digital nation.” Seen from the air it is a ring of land in a backdrop of blue, a thin coral halo sinking rapidly. Tuvalu will not accept its fate as a victim; it will not just give into the inevitable end handed to it by the global forces of destruction.

Radical hope is possible, Lear writes, because we can have courage. Courage is an important virtue because it recognizes that we are “finite erotic creatures. … As finite creatures we are vulnerable: we may suffer physical and emotional injury, we may make significant mistakes, even the concepts with which we understand ourselves and the world may collapse — and yet as erotic creatures we reach out to the world and try to embrace it.”

I caught the last light of the day at the church in Mundesley. The golden sun escaped from underneath the granite clouds and it washed the world gold. Just for a moment. A great rainbow arced overhead, a sign of hope and peace after the storm, the color that returned after the biblical flood.

There may not be a world of pure hope for these coastal villages, because there will be losses. Even with an ending, we can consider what practices of courage, care and value to adopt, and what can be salvaged as we build defenses, remember and protect elsewhere. The economy of salvation is never straightforward, so reach out and embrace the world even as it disappears.

stories.title: Scientists Are Teaching Birds to Sing Lost Songs
stories.summary: When bird populations decline, fledglings may struggle to learn the songs they need to attract mates. But new research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A rufous-collared sparrow. Charles J. Sharp via Wikipedia

When bird populations decline, fledglings may struggle to learn the songs they need to attract mates. But new research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs.

Listening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area.

That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song.

There is a growing recognition of birdsong’s importance to conservation, and of the need to better understand how birds learn to sing. If an individual sings well, and in a familiar “dialect,” they are better placed to find a mate, defend their territory, and ultimately survive.

If a species’ population declines, however, there are fewer opportunities for fledglings to become good singers. Birds can begin to tweet abnormally or mistakenly learn the songs of other species , jeopardizing their chances of breeding.

Male birds are in a better position to attract a mate if they can sing well — which, broadly speaking, means their song is complex, sung consistently, and well performed. “If your song requires a lot of energy, you might have to be in quite a good condition to sing it,” says Rebecca Lewis, a conservation scientist at Chester Zoo.

“When people talk about biodiversity, we’re always talking about genes, about genetic material,” says Gabriel B. Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, who coauthored the study on rufous-collared sparrows, and whose work is featured in a Guardian-produced documentary, Dream of Birds .

But animals’ learned behavior or culture, such as birdsong, is also an essential part of their population, says Mindlin.

The rufous-collared sparrow is not considered vulnerable globally, but researchers hope that synthetic recordings could help teach birdsong to other species whose populations are dwindling, allowing conservationists to tutor individuals where real-life recordings do not exist.

About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds (or oscine passerines), such as finches, sparrows, and blackbirds, which generally have complex songs that are at least partly learned from other individuals. Their songs are hugely diverse, though separate research on the wider passerine group of birds, which incorporates songbirds, has identified common “motifs” or building blocks: three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes, and harmonic notes.

The way that birds use these motifs reflects the environment in which the birds evolved. Flat whistles are more likely to be sung by birds in tropical rainforests where sound must travel through dense vegetation. Complex motifs, such as ultrafast trills, are more common in temperate regions where birds tend to communicate at closer range.

The song studied by Mindlin was recreated based on hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs that were made in the 1960s. Each song consists of a trill, which is consistent among individuals in the same region, and a theme, which varies. Some of the themes recorded decades ago are still sung by the local birds, but others have died out.

It is not clear why the song studied by Mindlin had disappeared, though he notes the population of birds in the park had declined.

Birds’ songs can change naturally over time — for example, birds might make errors when learning songs, which then can become imprinted in future renditions. Human encroachment and population declines can also cause dramatic changes.

Songbirds learn from other members of their species — such as a father or neighbors — which results in local groups developing their own dialects. The window for learning varies from a few weeks to a lifetime. Some species also have an innate level of knowledge.

“There’s such a diversity in songbirds in how they learn,” says Sarah Collins, associate professor of animal behavior at the University of Plymouth, who studied a group of cirl buntings that were translocated from Devon to Cornwall as part of a conservation project.

Initially, the birds produced abnormal songs that were squeaky and slow, and far less diverse than those of the source populations in Devon. “They didn’t have the richness of sound,” says Collins. Eight years later, however, their songs had returned to normal.

A few of the chicks were played recordings of cirl sounds, though not all. The study suggests that recovery of song is possible, though it is unclear if other species would bounce back in the same way. Cirl buntings are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the “notes” used in their songs, says Collins. “What they learn is how to put those elements together,” she says.

Some songbird species have a similar genetic underpinning and so may also be able to recover their songs, but others do not. Either way, Collins recommends a tutor to help other birds that are being translocated.

A separate study in Australia tracked regent honeyeaters that were bred in zoos to boost a critically endangered wild population that had fallen to about 250 individuals. Interacting with just two wild-born male “tutors” helped the zoo-bred birds to learn to sing the wild songs. Thereafter, zoo-bred males that had learned the traditional songs went on to tutor the next generation.

“Sometimes birds don’t learn very well from CDs or just playbacks. They need some sort of interaction,” says Collins.

Bringing wild birds into captivity to teach hand-reared chicks could cause huge distress and bring disease, however, risking the health of individuals from an already endangered population. It is possible that A.I. could help provide live tutoring in the future.

Dialect is also important. Past translocation projects have shown that birds are slower to match if they do not sing in the same dialect. “Birds with mismatched songs don’t pair quite as quickly or do quite as well once they’re paired,” adds Lewis. Familiarizing birds with songs of their destination can help to mitigate this.

A huge volume of birdsong is now being recorded and uploaded into databases, including by a growing number of hobbyists interested in birdwatching, says Mindlin. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says. “I don’t think we still have an idea that really we have to register dialects and communication systematically.”

In Buenos Aires, the song from the 1960s can still be heard. “It’s still being sung by just a few individuals, pretty close to where we inserted it,” he says, though only time will tell how long it persists.

— Rebecca Ratcliffe , The Guardian

stories.body:
The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies

W hen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.

“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China . “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”

She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario.

Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”

Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”.

Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.

At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.

“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”

It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.

The offerings are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.

Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.

In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.

‘A new generation of travellers’

“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction.

In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.

In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.

“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”

Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.

In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”.

Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.

“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.

Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.

*Name has been changed

stories.body:
Global cooperation seems unlikely despite AI increasing the risk of digital fraud and the need to protect the financial system

R ogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackers accessed their fridge controls and turned up the temperature to 50C.

Speaking at the fund’s annual meetings in the Thai capital, she was keen to hammer home the importance of guarding against “bad actors” in a rapidly changing, interconnected world – especially now that AI was “putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids”.

Policymakers have been warning for some time that the AI boom could at some point threaten financial stability via a share price crash – a “correction”, as it is euphemistically called.

But a different, related threat came into sharp focus in Bangkok. Georgieva said she was concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system altogether.

Social media feeds are rife with adverts using celebrity fakes to punt cryptocurrencies or gold, and even the old-school email-style scams can be generated far more prolifically.

Just as a sea of AI slop has the potential to undermine trust in fact-based reporting and send people down political rabbit holes, Georgieva fretted that cyber-fraud could knock consumer confidence in mainstream banks.

Recalling her own childhood behind the iron curtain in Bulgaria, she said many people did not trust the system, and kept their cash in a shoebox under the bed. “I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve … we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds,” she said.

It might not even take a cybercrime wave. This week the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, warned that the bank would not allow digital agents to operate on its customers’ behalf. “You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” he said.

AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, are starting to offer their users the opportunity to hand over their financial details. The agents will then scout for the highest savings rates and shift the user’s money accordingly.

Financial regulators fret about this for a number of reasons. One is that if such services become widely used, they could have destabilising herding effects. With deposits able to be moved around the financial system at a moment’s notice, it could accelerate a bank run in times of uncertainty.

A second worry is that highlighted by Dimon: who is responsible if your AI agent makes a financial decision on your behalf that turns out to be disastrous – or even criminal?

The answer is probably that we will need case law to find out, which will only come when something goes badly awry.

That is alarming because legal ambiguity about who owes what to whom when things go wrong can be an accelerant to financial instability.

We learned that lesson back in the 2008 financial crisis, when it turned out that some banks had built financial products with such fiendishly complex liability structures that they were effectively impossible to value – unleashing panic.

after newsletter promotion

Speaking alongside Georgieva, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board of global central bankers, pointed to another arresting news story from this week – that Anthropic had warned AI models might soon be able to “self-replicate” in domestic devices . Who should bear the responsibility – and the costs – if your internet-enabled oven, or telly, blows up as a result?

One entirely prudent response might be for consumers to reject internet-enabled devices and stick to “dumb” appliances instead that can’t be hijacked by self-replicating bots. This month, some of those French supermarkets rushed to take their fridges offline to avoid the hack.

While it may not be much of a loss to society if internet-enabled kettles and fridges do not take off, the financial analogue to a dumb appliance would be Georgieva’s shoeboxes – and that would have costs for those consumers, and the smooth running of the economy as a whole.

As Bailey somewhat apocalyptically put it: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”

Senior financial policymakers are genuinely disturbed at the collision between rapidly developing AI and the global financial system – which now extends well beyond heavily regulated banks – to embrace social media platforms, payments apps and other financial tools.

It is unfortunate this moment comes as the US – the crucible of the AI boom – is governed by a man whose main contribution to the debate has been to seek to rename AI “superintelligence” .

At the Bangkok meetings this week, Kevin Warsh, the chair of the US Federal Reserve, obediently used Donald Trump’s phrase on stage – as all US government agencies have been ordered to.

There has been some progress in acknowledging the risks. Trump’s superintelligence taskforce, chaired by the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, is setting up mechanisms for AI labs to report “breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other ​issues” – although not, it seems, to submit their models for pre-launch testing.

The UK has pledged to take up the issue of AI safety as part of its agenda for the G20 presidency next year, and G7 finance ministers announced in Bangkok that they would carry out simulations to test the resilience of the global financial system to cyber-attacks.

That could help to highlight vulnerabilities, but the questions at stake are much wider and more complex than whether criminals can hack the banks – and are urgent now, just as the prospects for international cooperation seem bleak. Superintelligence will seem anything but super if its misuse becomes a trigger for financial chaos.

stories.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
stories.summary: The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a blockbuster stock market listing.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Jack Clark, a co-founder and Head of Public Benefit of Anthropic

Published 19 October 2026, 03:41 BST

Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn).

The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market.

None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added.

Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday.

Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI , with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document , making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".

stories.body:
Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades

The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence.

While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs.

Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose.

“We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said.

“Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.”

Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language.

“There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.”

He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector.

The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand.

Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed.

She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work.

“If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.”

The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection.

after newsletter promotion

Georgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers.

“When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.”

Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work.

Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets.

“We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.

stories.title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
stories.summary: Trading standards officers say AI is "super-charging" existing scams through clones and fake websites.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 hours ago

Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.

Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.

If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say.

AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.

For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist , external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

What are the tricks to look out for?

Tricks include:

Cloned or new websites that look polished and professional in rapid time and at a low cost

Romance scams in which AI is used to remember victims' personal details and keep conversations going over weeks or months

AI-generated deepfake videos and voice-cloned audio is used to impersonate family members or close friends asking for money in an "emergency"

Error-free, personalised phishing emails, text messages and social media posts can be generated by AI on a huge scale

How can I protect myself?

Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI.

Typos or grammatical errors can no longer be relied on to spot scams, says consumer group Which?.

Some of the ways to protect yourself, according to trading standards, include:

Never sending money, gift cards or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in person

Doing your research - such as checking whether a shop's address is real, using the Financial Conduct Authority's Firm Checker , external , to ensure a company is authorised to give financial advice, and contacting a business directly to check whether a job advert is real

Not assuming someone is genuine just because you've heard their voice or seen them on a video call

In general, they say stop and think before paying, sharing personal information or taking action. You should be especially wary of pressure or urgency because criminals want you to act before you have time to think.

Fraud and scams can be reported to Report Fraud , external or by calling on 0300 1232040, or you can call the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline on 0808 223 1133 for advice.

stories.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
stories.summary: More property asking prices are being cut than at any time in 15 years, data shared with the BBC shows.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 hours ago

Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home.

Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price.

The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023.

Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed.

With mortgage rates at a three-year high , Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable.

So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed.

September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year.

Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price.

The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell.

Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Rightmove.

'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak? Published 19 September

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it Published 28 September

Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England.

One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier."

Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home".

But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget.

Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial.

"That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said.

Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price.

"The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said.

But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it.

In Scotland, the Home Report system , external requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market.

Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain.

His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London.

He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England.

stories.body:
Hot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomes

After a year marked by extreme heat and war sending fuel prices skywards, British travel executives hoped for solace in Madeira’s benign subtropical climate, separated by hundreds of miles of blue sea from the overtourism protests and six-hour EU-entry queues seen on the Portuguese mainland.

As bosses admitted, holidays will be ever less affordable, AI is coming for their jobs, and the visitable world is shrinking – not least those parts where tourists remain welcome.

Some of the bigger anxieties in spring , such as widespread border chaos and planes running out of fuel, have not come to pass; others now appear chronic issues. New supplies of jet fuel, a major concern after the US first attacked Iran in February, have been established – but the cost is staying far higher for longer than most expected.

“Fuel is a huge part of any holiday and people are going to have to reckon with the cost,” said Neil Swanson, Tui UK & Ireland managing director, among the attendees at the Abta convention.

Tui and airlines such as easyJet and Ryanair escaped the worst immediate impact by having secured much of their 2026 fuel supply at a fixed price. But the latter airlines are now slashing capacity for winter.

“It’s not great for consumers, who are going to have to pay a lot more for their holidays. But airlines are going to be less and less hedged and prices are going to go up,” Swanson added.

The oil price impact goes beyond jet fuel, said Mark Tanzer, the chief executive of Abta: “The bigger worry is the squeeze on household incomes that’s going to come through their domestic costs. It will be a much tighter market.”

Perhaps surprisingly, numbers have held up – but customers have been leaving it ever later to book, he said, whether in search of a deal or because of uncertainty from disruption, war or weather.

Despite the intense heat, mass travel firms are clear that the template has not changed: most customers still want a hot holiday, in summer, on the beach.

Garry Wilson, the chief executive of easyJet Holidays, said: “Will there be long-term effects on demand? Perhaps. But in the short-term, no, we don’t see it.”

Growing “shoulder season” travel outside the school holidays for those who can, including city breaks, are driven by price more than climate, several people suggest. And talk of “coolcations” or people turning towards northern climes cuts little ice here. “We’re not seeing any of that,” said Swanson. “Nothing’s changed, the destinations are the same.”

When Tunisia was forecast a 10-day stretch of 45C temperatures this summer, Tui offered customers the chance to switch their holiday elsewhere. Swanson said: “We didn’t get the interest and take-up. People were expecting it to be hot and were happy to go there, and we’re not seeing any change in demand. Brits like a warm holiday – if it’s got a pool and air-conditioning, that works for them.”

Neither does Wilson see many heading north. Citing easyJet destinations such as Tromsø in Norway or Malmö in Sweden, he said: “They’re all very nice to launch, but we send more customers to Majorca in a week than those in a year.”

Outbound holidays prospered in the heatwave, he suggested. “People thought: ‘You know what, we maybe don’t need to go away.’ But it became apparent that the UK doesn’t have the infrastructure to cope … people actually were going abroad to escape the heat in the UK.”

For now, the big firms see little change in destinations, Swanson said, but added: “We’ll keep it under review. Who knows where the temperature’s going to go in the next few years?”

More people could get priced out. At last year’s convention, the Spanish tourist board started pushing its cooler northern destinations; but, said Tanzer, “I’m not sure the north has 100m beds” to accommodate the visitors who predominantly go to Spain’s south, east and islands.

He added: “Certain types of holiday could become more expensive just because there’s limited availability. If the snow is higher up the mountain, there’s going to be fewer skiing holidays and the price is going to go up – there’s little room at the top.”

Tui has not been immune. Its river cruises in Europe were marooned when the Danube’s water levels dipped last month to the point where some passengers spent most of their return Austro-Hungarian cruise on a boat-replacement bus.

Katy Berzins, the head of river cruises at Tui, said: “Every year has highs and lows and it’s part of river cruising, rivers are changeable.” But 2026, she said, was “unprecedented”.

The division is expanding nonetheless. Two new ships are joining its fleet – initially destined for the Seine and the Douro – that are built with lower draught levels (the vessel’s vertical depth below the surface), meaning they are able to keep sailing in shallower rivers.

Others are seeing faster change. James Thornton, the chief executive of Intrepid Travel, said the firm no longer sold active travel group tours in southern Europe in the summer; few had wanted to trek or cycle in that level of heat.

Last year, Thornton said, there were 185 different extreme weather-related incidents that affected Intrepid holidaymakers around the world. “When we first started, there would be a handful.”

Intrepid has long wrestled with its own impact on climate: for years, before offsetting fell into disrepute, it paid millions to offset its emissions. That did not cover the biggest factor, the flights taken by its customers to reach Intrepid tours – not entirely dissimilar from how an airport might declare itself net zero. Instead now the firm has a decarbonisation fund for local projects: “Ultimately you can’t have sustainable travel, you can only limit the impact,” Thornton said.

Having grown from backpacking to a A$1bn annual business, its own footprint is becoming significant. This year the firm is launching Timor-Leste, or East Timor. Thornton said: “Some customers have done 30 to 40 trips, so they’re often looking for places that they haven’t been able to travel to.”

Asked about overtourism, Thornton said: “We’re definitely worried about it.” Intrepid tries to advertise the less visited destinations, he added. “We call it the not-hot list – drawing out the places where the infrastructure is available and the locals are willing to welcome travellers.”

Rising tourist taxes around the world underline that many places feel they have more than enough visitors. For Wilson, it is “grossly unfair”; destinations such as Mallorca, he said, “built enormous economic positions on the back of mass tourism, and then pull up the bridge and put on an extra tax. All that does is go back to the days of travel being only for the rich.”

How many of the UK outbound travel industry remain in sufficient paid work to afford it may also be in question.

Shaun Morton, the chief executive of On the Beach, laid off 20% of the Manchester-based online agency’s staff this summer to “automate and streamline” processes. He told delegates: “You’ve got the technology, people, processes and you hold them all dear … We just started to ask not how do we get 10% more out of that, but how do we get 10 times that, you know?”

He added that “very bright people with a sharp head with technology” probably would keep their jobs longest, but acknowledged: “They’re worried, because they can see a little bit further ahead than everyone else.”

stories.body:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package

No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.

Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .

The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.

The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.

The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.

This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.

They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”

Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.

EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.

But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.

Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.

According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.

This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.

Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.

A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.

China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.

While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.

Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.

At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.

Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.

“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

Supporters of planned tax, however, say banks were bailed out by taxpayers during financial crisis and can afford to pay more now

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget

The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.

Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.

Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.

He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.

He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”

Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week.

City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad.

In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group.

It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been.

He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%.

“The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.”

However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023.

At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders.

Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits.

after newsletter promotion

Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year.

“The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday.

While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways.

“Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam.

Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks.

But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others.

“But they always say this, [and] they rarely move. I think that if the chancellor judges this right, with a moderate increase in taxation or some other form of getting money from the banks, then the business will remain in the UK.”

How architects worked with harsh environment to create sustainable building in location where fossils were found

V iewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China , the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen.

Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment.

The Hami region is notorious for its scorching summers. Air temperatures can exceed 55C (131F), while the surface ground temperature can reach 80C, says Wang Xiaolin, the director of the museum and a palaeontologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Violent winds and sandstorms terrorise the area frequently, according to Xiaolin, who has carried out excavation work in Hami for 20 years.

Despite the intimidating conditions, building the museum in the area is important from a scientific perspective because this is where the fossils were buried and found, Xiaolin says. Keeping the fossils local protects the fragile relics and lets visitors see them in their geological context, he adds.

Visitors to the five exhibition halls can expect to see precious fossils discovered by Xiaolin’s team, including one that has preserved the upper and lower jaws, as well as the soft-tissue structures of the head crest of a pterosaur that roamed the area roughly 130m years ago.

Most of the 8,000-sq metre museum is built 8 metres into the ground where temperatures are much lower, which helps it stay cool in summer, says Huai Kaifeng, an architect at Beijing-based Turenscape, which designed the project. In winter, when temperatures can drop below -20C, the design also helps the museum stay warm.

Being largely underground, with seven above-ground entrances, allows the museum to use its energy as efficiently as possible, says Wang Yujia, a landscape architect and associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in the US, who is not involved in the project. Most of it is able to avoid direct exposure to wind, sand and solar heat and the large temperature swings between day and night in the desert. “This all means that you need much, much less air-conditioning,” Yujia says.

Although air-conditioners have been installed to provide backup, the museum has natural ventilation shafts that allow cool air to sink and hot air to rise and escape. The museum can cut its electricity usage on air conditioning by 94% compared with an above-ground counterpart, according to estimates by Turenscape. This equates to a saving of 223,421kWh of electricity annually – enough to power an average UK home for 89 years.

But the underground space in the desert presented another challenge for the architects: lighting. The team used giant, translucent, ceiling-to-floor funnels to let in as much natural light as possible. These structures slash the museum’s need for artificial lighting by nearly 50%, saving 84,672kWh of electricity a year, according to Turenscape.

The museum was one of the last designs completed by the late Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu , the founder of Turenscape. Yu was the brain behind China’s “ sponge cities ”, a concept that uses nature to prevent flooding in urban areas.

after newsletter promotion

The museum has its own micro power grid, featuring a solar farm and batteries to store energy. The solar farm is about 1km from the museum, with an outline resembling that of a pterosaur when viewed from above. It is expected to generate more than 22.4GWh of electricity a year, enough to meet the museum’s own demand, Huai says. The museum is still connected to the power grid of the nearby city of Hami to ensure its energy security, he notes.

The museum is also connected to Hami’s water-supplying network, but it has a recycling system on site to collect, process and reuse its grey water.

“Water is precious out here in the Gobi,” Xiaolin says.

For Yujia, the museum is a good example of how a building can be designed to adapt to its natural environment rather than fight against it.

Although technology enables people to build luxury resorts in a desert and keep them cool, such projects require huge amounts of energy and resources, he says.

“It makes sense to work as much as possible with the environmental conditions that are already there, instead of relying entirely on technology to isolate the building from them.”

Examples include a floating exhibition pavilion built in Rotterdam to address rising sea levels, and a giant park with a tilted ground in Bangkok that aims to prevent urban flooding, and a home shaped like a snail’s shell in Iran to help its inhabitants stay cool.

The concept is important for arid areas. “These places are not cities, you don’t necessarily have the basic infrastructure or the resources you desire even if you pay, because money is not magic,” Yujia adds.

Designing buildings and parks to combat natural disasters was a lasting theme throughout Yu’s career, and for Jiinyi Hwang, the chief architect at Turenscape, the museum is no exception.

“Our world is drying. Deserts and arid zones are expanding. Cities are warming. More and more of the built environment is being pushed into climates that were once considered unbuildable,” Hwang says. “If we keep designing with the same assumptions – sealed boxes, glass facades and mechanical climate control – we will consume the very resources these landscapes cannot spare.”

Nscale said it remained committed to building a £2bn AI data centre in Loughton

Published 18 October 2026

A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project.

Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton , Essex.

However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement.

A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment.

"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said.

"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term."

What is the new AI supercomputer planned for Essex? Published 18 September 2025

The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year.

But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday , external , Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.

"This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC.

Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.

The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens.

Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer.
