stories.title: Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses
stories.summary: At the IMF meeting in Bangkok this week finance and business leaders grappled with uncertainty.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 October 2026

When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.

At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.

In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget Published 4 days ago

'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK Published 8 October

Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF Published 5 days ago

But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.

Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs.

It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.

This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.

The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.

Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".

It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump.

But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.

Shevaun Haviland argues PM is right to revisit Labour’s EU red lines as current trading relationship is bad for business

Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said.

Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business.

“We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said.

Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit , Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them.

“We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said.

Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far , with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product.

At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty” .

In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit .

She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU.

“We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now.

“We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.”

Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’”

after newsletter promotion

Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East.

Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market .

“This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said.

“You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?”

Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said.

“The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”

Healey quizzed about bank tax plans

Over at the IMF’s annual meeting in Bangkok today, chancellor John Healey is meeting with UK journalists now, including my colleague Heather Stewart .

Healey , who should be cheered by the news that the UK economy grew unexpectedly in August , was asked whether he plans to impose new taxes on the bank sector, and replies:

double quotation mark “I don’t want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks’ time. My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects. That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

Healey added that his “special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future” – echoing what he told Sky News a few minutes ago .

The chancellor also welcomed the IMF’s support for the UK’s fiscal plans.

Closing post

Time to wrap up.

The US inflation squeeze has intensified, with new data showing that US producer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in more than four years.

With higher energy costs hitting the US economy, the producer price index advanced 1.3% from a month earlier — the most since March 2022. On an annual basis, prices were 6.3% higher.

The data helped to push down shares on Wall Street, as an accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.

Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.

US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell , which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent , which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.

The UK rallied, though, helped by the news that Britain’s economy kept growing.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction.

With less than a fortnight before the budget, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.

John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules.

Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.

Healey also hailed the contribution that UK banks make, calling them part of the ‘jewel in the crown’ – amid speculation that he could impose higher taxes on them in the budget.

He told reporters:

double quotation mark My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

Some Labour MPs want the chancellor to raise taxes on the gambling sector .

US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account

US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

FTSE 100 hits five-week high

The UK stock market is continuing to benefit from turmoil elsewhere.

The FTSE 100 share index is now up 1.1% at 10,843 points, its highest level since 8 September.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says US assets are acting like a ‘harbour in the storm’:

double quotation mark A stronger economy, combined with a resilient FTSE 100, which is the best performing major index so far this week, is good news for the pound and the Gilt market. As other markets crash and burn, the pound is the top performing G7 currency this week, and the Gilt market is the best performer amongst its peers on Thursday. When the AI trade sells off, the UK is the harbour in the storm.

The US economy is continuing to hold onto workers, despite inflationary pressures.

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment support remained low last week, at 199,000 - 1,000 more than a week earlier.

Coherent Corp , the US manufacturer of lasers, engineered materials, and optoelectronic components for AI data centres, is also caught up in the sell-off – its shares are down 9%.

Europe has to take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said.

Dan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing policy, said EU governments could choose actions to make fossil fuels cheaper as long as they were “targeted” and “temporary” so as not to derail the continent from its goal to tackle the climate crisis by drastically cutting carbon emissions.

Our Europe Live blog has all the details:

Dell (-9%) are leading the fallers on the S&P 500, as doubts persist about the AI boom.

That adds to their 11% drop yesterday, after analysts at Barclays raised concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won’t justify the AI buildout.

Wall Street opens in the red

Stocks are dropping on Wall Street at the start of trading, as inflation worries and AI angst hit share prices.

Tech stocks are leading the sell-off, pulling the Nasdaq index down by 1.3%.

The broader S&P 500 share index has dropped by 0.5%.

This morning’s jump in the US PPI index will have raised concerns about inflationary pressures.

Traders are also reacting to the sell-off in Asia-Pacific markets overnight, where South Korea’s Kospi hit a six-month low overnight ( see earlier post ).

On the AI front, AstraZeneca has entered into a new collaboration with a Californian AI therapeuticscompany called insitro , aimed at identifying novel targets to develop medicines for liver and heart disease.

The collaboration will focus on the areas of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a serious liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, diseases of the heart muscle.

Insitro has created a virtual human to generate large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design. The deal is worth $1.46bn, with $40m paid upfront by AstraZeneca . The Californian company also has partnerships with US drugmakers Bristol Myers-Squibb and Eli Lilly.

Sharon Barr , executive vice resident and head of biopharmaceuticals research & development at AstraZeneca , said:

double quotation mark “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximising the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”

Today’s jump in wholesale US inflation increases the pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates soon.

Waleed Said , technical analyst at GivTrade , says the increase in core PPI means the energy shock from the Iran war is spreading, adding:

double quotation mark A firmer Fed is more likely but the market pricing about a one in three chance of a hike in October so don’t overreact to the headline but a rate hike in December does seem imminent.

US PPI inflation driven up by soaring gasoline

Tin hats on!

New data from the US has shown that producers are hiking prices at their fastest rate in almost four years, and much faster than expected.

Ths increase was driven by a surge in energy prices, which more than wiped out a drop in egg prices.

The Producer Price Index, which measures how much goods makers and services firms charge for their wares, jumped by 6.3% in the year to September. That’s the largest 12-month increase since December 2022, when it rose by 6.4%.

On a monthly basis, prices climbed by 1.2% in September alone, a sign that inflationary pressures rose last month.

The report shows that goods prices jumped by 2.6% in September alone, the largest increase since data were first calculated in December 2009.

That was driven by the rise in motor fuel; The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports:

double quotation mark Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7 percent.

Alarmingly, core PPI also jumped. Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0% in the year to September.

PPI is an important measure, as increases in producer prices tend to be passed onto consumers, who already experienced a jump in inflation last month:

EU pushing for action over trade deficit with China

The EU is set to call for further action to curb the bloc’s vast trade deficit with China, widely blamed for job losses and factory closures across the continent.

EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the trade deficit with China - which hit €360bn in 2025 - are expected to call for “new instruments to better address these imbalances” according to a draft statement.

The European Commission, which negotiates trade policy on behalf of the 27 member states, agreed a deal this month with Beijing that will see the EU limit hybrid car exports from China to 350,000 vehicles a year, potentially halving Chinese market share.

EU countries have welcomed the deal, but think it is not enough and want steps to protect other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, plastics and machinery.

The debate has sharpened since Germany - long reluctant to use trade defences against China - converted to a more hawkish position amid pressure from German industrial leaders, who are laying off workers and closing factories.

Germany and France last week called for better use of existing trade defence measures, including urgent action in the chemicals and plastics sectors.

The EU’s two biggest economies are also seeking “a diversification instrument” that would cut off access to the EU market when faced with severe imbalances. Dubbed the “kill switch”, the law is intended to be country agnostic, but is clearly aimed at China.

Member states have welcomed the deal negotiated by EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič on hybrid cars, but are sceptical as to whether Beijing will stick to it. China would adhere to the agreement because they began to realise “they are killing their customers” , Šefčovič was reported to have said, according to a senior EU diplomat.

The EU diplomat highlighted the urgency of the situation from the EU’s point of view: “We don’t have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost.”

UK government says it is minded to intervene in Sky-ITV deal

Media news: The UK government is ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s£1.6bn deal to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm.

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, has told parliament she believes there are public interest grounds for intervening in the deal.

They include ‘the need for free expression of opinion in news media’, the need for a pluratity of views in the news, and the need for a wide range of broadcasting which is “of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests.”

Back in July, Sky said the deal was a chance to create a “UK-focused national streaming champion”.

Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to reduce food waste on farms

Published 18 October 2026

A gleaning group has saved £1m worth of fruit and vegetables that would have been left in field and donated them to food banks.

Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to collect unwanted produce from harvested fields, delivering it to 160 food banks, community larders and kitchens across the South West.

Despite reaching the seven-figure milestone, the group has warned more funding is needed in order to keep up with demand.

Reliance on food banks is increasing and since 2015 the number of known settings providing food aid in Cornwall has risen from 20 to 180, according to Cornwall Council.

The gleaning group has saved 460 tonnes of produce since the start of 2020

Gleaning Cornwall started in 2020 and said it had repurposed more than 460 tonnes of produce since then.

But the charity's founder, Holly Whitelaw, warned it was now threatened by economic constraints.

"There is less money around and we need to do more with it," she said. "Our infrastructure urgently needs funding if we are to keep going."

The charity said it fed 11,000 people every week with the stipulation that all its produce must be completely free to recipients.

However, the organisation said the cost of transport, storage and coordination was rising sharply.

More news stories for Cornwall

Listen to the latest news for Cornwall

It comes at a time when food bank usage is higher than ever with statistics from Cornwall's Trussell Trust showing its food banks distributed more than 35,500 emergency food parcels between April 2024 and March 2025.

A study by Cornwall Council found that 30% of children in the county are living in food poverty.

Whitelaw encouraged people to play their part by reducing the amount of food they wasted at home.

She said: "If we waste food, we waste the substantial energy that went into producing it.

"Utilising what we already have saves money and helps the environment."

stories.title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
stories.summary: Chancellor John Healey will set out his plans for UK taxes on 28 October.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 28 September 2026

Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.

He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited.

Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT.

What is the Budget?

In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes.

Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs.

The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future.

What might be in the Budget?

The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.

Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:

Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament

To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament

In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.

Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. KPMG believe it could have fallen to £12bn, mainly due to the rise in government borrowing costs this year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) also forecasts that debt interest will significantly reduce headroom. But it also suggests higher inflation could push up tax revenues as pay rises drag people into higher tax thresholds.

It estimates the buffer could still shrink but to a comparatively less severe £20bn.

One option that has been floated is that Healey could decide to accept a smaller buffer, reducing the need to increase taxes in the Budget.

Bank taxes

Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector . UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.

Your First Home scheme

Further details on the "Your First Home" scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Capital Gains Tax

There has been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions.

At the moment, if you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

The FT has reported , external that Healey has rejected proposals to raise CGT to the same rates as income tax.

Tax on businesses

The Times has reported , external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.

The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.

Fuel duty

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

Healey told the BBC in late September that the "place" and "time" for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.

Energy bills

Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276 .

There has been speculation , external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.

Mansion Tax

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the Mansion Tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.

There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest , external Healey has ruled this out.

How is the economy doing?

In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, while in the April-to-June quarter it grew by 0.5%.

The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.1% in August after growth of 0.4% in July, with both figures being stronger than expected.

Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.

The conflict has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas trade. This caused a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices.

Economists expect UK growth to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses.

Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.

The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row in September, but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

What time is the Budget and what happens afterwards?

The Budget speech usually starts at about 12:30 UK time - after Prime Minister's Questions - and lasts about an hour.

It will be broadcast live on the BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website.

The Leader of the Opposition, Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch, will respond to the speech in the House of Commons.

MPs debate the measures for four days, before voting on them.

If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately.

However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent.

stories.title: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise our coastal towns?
stories.summary: Engineer David Mummery has developed a tidal energy generator that he says can change lives for people living in coastal communities.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Engineer David Mummery says tidal power could change lives in coastal communities

Published 18 October 2026

In a secret location in the Highlands of Scotland, there's a fast-flowing river that's the key to understanding the massive power of water.

It's where engineer David Mummery found himself more than a decade ago.

With a length of cord tied tightly across the river, he swam out, gripped firmly, and let the unstoppable current rush over as he sunk his head below the surface.

"As an engineer we do the maths and stuff," he says, "but sometimes you can get a lot more from actually touching the water and feeling it".

As he lay down in the powerful rapids, he visualised a new type of small-scale tidal energy generator.

It's an innovation he says could change lives for people in coastal communities.

"I'd be under the river, feeling the turbulence of the water rushing over me.

"Trying to envisage how this turbine needed to interact with that environment - to understand the way the water was working."

The Swimmer Turbine prototype at Strangford Narrows in Northern Ireland

Mummery's idea became the Swimmer Turbine - a 50kw tidal generator named after his experience in the river.

Anchored to the sea floor, the fiberglass and steel device lies invisible below the water's surface. It can generate enough electricity to power about 30 homes.

He began tests in the river in early 2010s. On a patent lawyer's advice he found a secret location, far from curious Highland tourists and their cameras.

"You're trying to be quite discreet because you're working with new technology," he says.

It was in the first years of his company, Flex Marine Power, long before Britain was gripped by the soaring costs of an energy crisis.

Fishermen on Islay learn how to assemble the Swimmer Turbine

The size of the Swimmer Turbine is what sets it apart from large tidal projects dotted around Scottish waters.

Scotland is a world leader in the sector at sites including:

Nova Innovation - The world's first tidal stream array, deployed in 2016 in Bluemull Sound in Shetland

MeyGen - The world's largest tidal array, with four large 1.5MW turbines on the seabed of the Pentland Firth

Orbital O2 - The world's most powerful floating turbine, generating 2MW, anchored at Fall of Warness in the Orkney Islands

Mummery's turbine is ultra compact and low cost compared to these giant machines. Fishermen and local workers can build and install it themselves from their own village harbour.

"Can you imagine like an Ikea furniture kit? You get a shipping container and you'll open it up and it will be about 20 components.

"You'll bolt them all together and then you've got your turbine ready.

"There'll be a launch plan, you follow these instructions, then you'll be in the water."

Mummery's work did not always focus on small-scale power. Originally from Guildford, he studied mechanical engineering at Surrey University.

Before founding Flex Marine Power, he was a sought-after consultant in the UK energy sector. For a time he specialised in nuclear work and decommissioning, designing robots for pulling material out of contaminated tanks.

He moved north after falling in love with a girl studying at Glasgow University. Jo became his wife and they now live in the city suburbs with three young children.

Conveniently, Mummery's relocation came at a time when Scotland was establishing its reputation as a centre for marine power expertise.

The 180m-long Pelamis wave power project, nicknamed the sea snake

In 2010 he took a secondment at Scottish Power Renewables on the ground-breaking Pelamis project in Orkney.

The 180m-long (591ft) Pelamis P2 - nicknamed the sea snake - was the first deep-water, floating wave energy machine to generate power for the national grid.

Ultimately, Pelamis went into administration in 2014 , but the ill-fated device remains celebrated as a milestone in marine power innovation.

"The industry is littered with these examples of fantastic technologies and teams that do brave things that take decades," Mummery says.

"But at some point the market doesn't step up and they falter. Some really good ones have lasted the course, but others have not and it's sad."

David Mummery at home in Glasgow, where he established Flex Marine Power

Mummery says the UK has "phenomenal waters for tidal power" and he loved being a part of major projects - but couldn't shake a discomfort.

His work felt incongruous to the many small coastal communities he found himself in.

"I'd be going out on boats around Scotland doing sonar surveys with all these really expensive pieces of kit.

"But the equipment was all really big, utility-scale stuff that would weigh hundreds of tonnes, shipped by people from the mainland.

"All the people I was meeting in harbours or in the pub were fishermen. And they were knowledgeable and they were interested.

"I thought 'we've got to do this in a way that they can take the lead'."

That, he says, is what motivated his Swimmer Turbine idea.

The Swimmer Turbine is assembled on land and can be launched from a slipway

In 2011 he left big projects behind to found Flex Marine Power and focus on his turbine concept.

He spent hours at his desk sketching, working out how to make the technology smaller and lighter.

He hired a student employee and found a sleek, glass office space outside Glasgow - which he quickly discovered wasn't entirely suited to an engineer and his tools.

"It was a lovely place, but I wasn't allowed to take a hammer drill into the office.

"We were trying to make prototype turbines under the desk so the landlord wouldn't see them when he came in."

Learning the ropes, the local team in training off the coast of Islay

Mummery turned to Clydeside's shipbuilding past in search of a more suitable workspace.

He presented a plan to convert former shipyards for marine technology research, and was invited to Greenock by Inverclyde's redevelopment authority.

"There were lots of empty sheds that hadn't been used for years," he says.

"They basically said 'we'll walk you around, you can pick a shed'. So I got the pick of the bunch right on the quayside."

Mummery now had direct access to the River Clyde for sea trials to test his models.

He developed a prototype which he successfully trialled in 2015 on the island of Luing, in the Firth of Lorn, near Oban.

It secured Flex Marine's first major investment and expansion the following year.

The Swimmer turbine can be installed without large cranes or heavy lift equipment

The next major step was in Northern Ireland in 2020, at Strangford Narrows in County Down.

Mummery worked with Queen's University Belfast who had an academic license to test tidal equipment at sea.

"Me and Mark, my accountant, lifted all of the components into a shipping container and sent it out on a lorry.

"We were introduced to a bunch of local mariners. We pulled off a full-scale tidal turbine installation out of a container deposited in a farmyard."

Generating electricity while tethered to the back of a boat, Mummery says it was the full-scale proof-of-concept that "finally put us on the map".

It helped Flex Marine Power secure £968,000 from the UK government's Energy Entrepreneurs Fund for a team of nine people to develop a commercial turbine model.

This version would not be tied to a boat.

The Swimmer Turbine would launch directly from shore and remain absolutely hidden, generating electricity below the surface of the water.

The waters of Islay are perfect for whisky and the tidal energy industry

Mummery took it through months of testing last year on the island of Islay - famous for its many whisky distilleries and coastal waters that are perfect for tidal power.

He rented space at a boatyard where "talented local people" were taught how to assemble and launch the device.

Finally, after his years of work, came the defining moment.

"I was standing at the end of the slipway, seeing our machine, without any of my guys touching it.

"It was all local people. Fishermen, using their own tractor, launching it down their own slipway. This was my vision in a nutshell."

Assembled from a shipping container, the turbine is invisible below the water surface

The next stage is putting the power to good use. Mummery will return to Islay next year with a plan to generate electricity for the island.

"The sea is a very big space and these things are invisible. There could be different tidal arrays in different parts of the island, all owned by different people.

"In those real coastal communities, they don't have flashy cranes and heavy lifting capabilities and big corporate companies with big pockets.

"But what they do have is knowledge and work ethic and a deep understanding of their environment and the sea.

"We're trying to equip real people to thrive by giving them access to the power that's in the tides."

stories.summary: Zoey Darnbrough had no idea there was a distillery near her home - now she has a top tourism role there.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Zoey Darnbrough took a job at Annandale Distillery after finishing her studies

Published 18 October 2026

Zoey Darnbrough is the first to admit that just a few years ago she did not even know there was a whisky distillery near her hometown in southern Scotland.

But it hasn't stopped her rising rapidly from tour guide, to group tourism and events co-ordinator at the site near Annan.

She went away to study heritage and tourism in Stirling after school, but unlike many of her peers, she returned to Dumfries and Galloway for work.

Now she hopes to play her part in changing people's opinions of the world of whisky "one woman at a time".

Annandale distillery shut in 1919 before reopening 90 years later

The 26-year-old, who attended St Joseph's College in Dumfries, was recently nominated for "rising star" recognition at the South of Scotland Thistle Awards.

Zoey said her journey had not been straightforward as she did not get the exam results she had hoped for at school, so she spent time working in the kitchens at Dumfries Infirmary.

But when a job came up at Annandale Distillery, she jumped at the chance.

She said: "My first thought was - there's a distillery in Annan? And my second thought was - whisky?

"I thought I'd give it a chance and see what it was like because there's a lot of heritage when it comes to whisky.

"And I've now been here three-and-a-half years and I've not looked back."

Revived distillery toasts first 10-year-old malt Published 25 November 2024

Whisky wait is over after 99 years Published 15 November 2017

What does she think the area has to offer that others her age might ignore?

One thing she highlighted was the relative costs of property compared with city prices.

Zoey also believes the area has a lot to shout about and is happy to have returned after university.

"The south of Scotland has so much heritage and it is a passion of mine," she said.

"So I would naturally like to be somewhere where there's a lot of heritage and where I can kind of grow as an individual."

Zoey is passionate about what the south of Scotland has to offer

But she agrees that a lot more could be done to stop young people from leaving.

"I would like to think we could go back to the local schools across the region and try and explain that there are other careers out there including in heritage and tourism," she said.

Zoey would also like to see the area market itself better.

"We've got so much to offer in terms of castles, in terms of scenery, in terms of attractions, accommodation, it's so vast," she said.

"I always like to say that we've got everything that the Highlands have, but just in a much quieter area.

"But we're going to use that quietness to our strength."

Get in touch

What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland?

She has certainly achieved that in her own career in the whisky industry - despite some people assuming she might lack the knowledge of older, male counterparts.

"It has been tricky, I'm not going to lie," she said. "But I always think that if you prepare yourself well, those types of questions cannot faze you.

"I've been so fortunate that all my experiences have been mostly pleasant and so I have not really felt it, but I do understand the struggles that other people face.

"We just need to start changing people's opinions one woman at a time."

Zoey is happy to do that from Dumfries and Galloway for the foreseeable future.

"I'm only beginning to stick my teeth into the south of Scotland," she said. "So to leave, it would have to be a fairly big jump."

Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire

Published 5 hours ago

Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.

Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity".

"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.

The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.

Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.

Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.

Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.

"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.

A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.

"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Incident at Canadian military base 'unheard of', says local mayor

Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.

News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.

Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".

The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.

In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".

Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".

What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base Published 3 hours ago

Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.

Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.

The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down.

Wainwright is about 200km (125 miles) from Edmonton, the provincial capital

The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units.

"It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province.

STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed.

Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance.

Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said.

"I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie".

stories.title: Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
stories.summary: Alan Feeney was captured on undercover filming calling Asian homeowners "parasites".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alan Feeney has stepped down as deputy mayor of Solihull, and given up his role as a councillor in both Solihull and Birmingham

Published 16 October 2026

Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

A Reform UK councillor filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites" has resigned from two councils and apologised for his comments.

Alan Feeney, who has since stepped down from the party, was heard making the remarks during undercover filming for an ITV News investigation , external in the run up to council elections in May.

Feeney said he had resigned every post he held on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, adding that his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".

He has also been suspended from his job with the prison service, with the Ministry of Justice [MoJ] describing the comments captured during the documentary as "despicable".

In July, his register of interests with Solihull council recorded he was employed as a custodial manager, a position described on the HM Prison and Probation Service website as "the most senior uniformed officers in a prison".

Feeney was one of several Reform members featured in the ITV investigation, which was gathered over the course of a year.

In it, while campaigning in the run-up to May's elections, Feeney described an area as "infested" with Asian families and called them "absolute parasites".

He was also recorded saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.

'Unreserved apologies'

Writing on Facebook on Friday, Feeney said he wanted "to offer my sincere and unreserved apologies for the comments I made in the recording that has recently come to light".

He added the comments did "not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report".

These were communities he had "supported countless times" over many years, he added.

He stated his true self was reflected in more than a decade of public service, but achievements "cannot reduce the impact of what has been said".

Feeney, who defected from the Conservative Party to Reform last year, was elected to the Shard End ward on Birmingham City Council in May.

A spokesperson for Reform Solihull said Feeney was briefly with the party, but spent the majority of his time as a Conservative councillor, and did not reflect "the views of the group".

The MoJ has stated the comments featured in the documentary would be investigated and action taken in line with its policy.

By-elections in Solihull

Undercover reporters also filmed with two other Reform candidates in Solihull - Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan.

On Friday, Solihull Council's leader of the opposition, Reform's Samantha Gethen, said all three councillors had now resigned, which "was the right thing to do", adding that there would now be by-elections.

Comments reported this week "were offensive, hurtful and wrong", Gethen said.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Friday , Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.

He added that all parties had "bad apples" and denied it was any more of a problem in Reform than other parties.

On Thursday, the party told the BBC that Feeney had "mutually agreed" to resign from the party.

stories.body:
Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last

I nside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy.

A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King.

“Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared.

Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development.

Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO).

According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP.

It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict.

The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies.

Aside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks.

The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic.

That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time.

“Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said.

Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth.

The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva , lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.”

Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another.

The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting of G20 finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year.

The UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates.

The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence.

“The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny.

“Traditionally we’ve seen more attention, in relative terms in the UK, to what the government is doing. [There is] a bit more sensitivity, and I think the government recognises they need to stay the course.”

Unusually, no communique was issued after the G20 meeting: a stark signal of how difficult it has become to reach multilateral agreement in the current fissiparous period.

The UK will take over the G20 presidency next year and has ambitious plans, on AI regulation and international development; but Bessent’s no-show was a reminder of the tough task they face in rekindling multilateralism.

The other alarming message the IMF was keen to land, concerned the threat of an AI market crash. As Georgieva put it in a blogpost on Friday: “The risk is that expectations may run rapidly ahead of productivity gains, setting the stage for near-term disappointment.”

The Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, while professing himself an optimist about the long-term gains of “superintelligence”, as he insisted on calling it, put it another way: “We really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies. Who’s going to get to make the money? What are the consequences for those that bet that they were going to make money, but the market structure doesn’t allow it?”

And AI is not just a stock market phenomenon but a huge driver of real-world exports, of the hardware and infrastructure necessary – albeit the benefits are heavily concentrated in a small number of economies, including Taiwan and South Korea. The knock-on effects, then, would be significant.

It is a familiar fear; but in its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Review, the IMF laid out in detail the rising levels of debt being used to finance the AI boom; the intricate financial linkages between the companies involved; and the increasingly leveraged position of the investors – including hedge funds – backing them up.

As far back as the Wall Street crash of almost a century ago, the economist JK Galbraith was highlighting the fact that leverage – betting with borrowed money, effectively – tends to amplify booms and busts.

And as ministers met in the Thai capital, elsewhere in Asia there were tremors that may suggest Georgieva’s fear of “near-term disappointment” may already be gripping some investors.

South Korea’s Kospi share index recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, tumbling by 14.5% during the week, as traders ditched chip manufacturers such as Samsung and SK Hynix.

Analysts reported that questions around the borrowing, spending commitments and future profitability of AI companies unsettled the markets. Bonds issued by the datacentre CoreWeave slumped almost to distressed levels as these worries swirled.

Expectations of future increases in US interest rates also rose, after data showing that consumer price inflation rose in September, as did inflation at the US factory gate. US tech stocks were also hit, knocking 2% off the Nasdaq index between Monday and Thursday.

It was just the latest of a series of market wobbles of late, and finance ministers and central bankers probably gave it little thought as they were whisked in air-conditioned comfort back to their capitals this weekend.

But if the boom does turn to bust, sending shock waves through the global economy, they won’t be able to say they weren’t warned that the “resilience” we have been enjoying rests on shaky foundations.

stories.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
stories.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 October 2026

US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".

Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday

Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.

Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.

The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.

Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.

However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.

Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

stories.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
stories.summary: On his first substantive trip to Scotland since becoming PM, he says politicians should focus on solutions "right now" and move beyond the issue of Scottish independence.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 October 2026

The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'

However, he described Scotland as the most devolved nation in the UK but "one of the most centralised in Europe".

"During my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland's regions and cities," he said.

"Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.

"This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people."

Burnham to visit Scotland during SNP conference Published 5 days ago

Burnham - Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas decisions coming 'shortly' Published 4 days ago

The Scottish government set out plans for a radical rethink of the country's regional authorities last month.

A new two-tiered system would see the 32 local authorities replaced with six new regional authorities .

They would have power over major issues such as economic growth and education.

Below that, between 120 and 160 community authorities would govern more local issues, such as licensing and town centre improvements.

It would be the most significant change to Scotland's regional makeup since the current system was introduced by the UK government in 1996.

Burnham acknowledged that the Scottish government was working on local government reform, but said this had to "move faster".

It is not clear exactly what powers might be exercised at regional level other than employment support.

Burnham appears to expect the Scottish government to devolve some of its own powers to regional authorities.

But he made clear that he will not impose a model of regional devolution like the metropolitan mayors that already operate in England.

Instead he wants to try and agree a way forward with further discussions when the prime minister sits down with all the devolved first ministers at the end of this month.

John Swinney denied that too much power was centralised at Holyrood

Burnham also called for an end to "tribal politics" between the Scottish and UK governments.

He said he and Swinney "agreed on some things" but "didn't have to agree on everything".

Swinney is expected to promote his renewed push for independence in his keynote speech at the SNP conference on Saturday.

He previously welcomed Burnham telling MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.

But Burnham later pushed back on that by telling Swinney at a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".

Asked whether devolving power more locally in Scotland would make independence more or less likely, the prime minister said: "I don't want to be the last PM of the UK.

"I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.

"In my view, people in Scotland are suffering from the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else, and I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people right now."

He added: "Too much time is wasted on those dramas, it consumes too much energy."

'As many powers as possible'

Stephen Flynn - who was the SNP's leader at Westminster before becoming the Transport Secretary at Holyrood - said the Scottish government would welcome the opportunity to be handed more power over the country's economic prospects.

He said: "Interestingly the first minister sent a letter to the prime minister on Monday where he outlined a number of points he would like to see engagement on.

"This was number seven on that list, so we will of course engage with the prime minister fully in respect of his announcement today."

Before Burnham's speech, First Minister John Swinney said he was interested in "working constructively" with Westminster, adding he was "all for the Scottish Parliament having as many powers" as possible.

UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham should be focusing on creating new opportunities in the energy sector.

She said: "This regional devolution plan is more jobs for the boys. What Andy Burnham should be doing is granting new oil and gas licences in the north sea."

"Devolution is a process, not a solution."

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top official in the Foreign Office in April

Published 16 October 2026

Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador.

Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir.

How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public.

It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him.

A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades".

A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters."

Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance.

Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time.

Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him."

Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential".

He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson.

He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management".

Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.

"The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat.

"We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process."

Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time.

"I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life".

Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.
